issues.legal_issue: A law authorizing compulsory acquisition for a public purpose cannot make the executive declaration of that purpose conclusive evidence of its existence.
material_facts: The challenged law authorized acquisition of land for public purposes, including settlement and development.
It made the government’s declaration that land was needed for a public purpose conclusive evidence of that fact.
The State conceded that the existence of a public purpose had to be established objectively.
issues.conclusion: The provision making the government’s declaration conclusive was unconstitutional and void.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) made the existence of a public purpose a necessary condition of acquisition, so that purpose had to be established objectively as a fact. The provision was not saved by Article 31(5), read with Article 31(6), because the law had been enacted within eighteen months before the Constitution commenced and had not received the certification required by Article 31(6).

predicates.public_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a law authorizing property to be acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.executive_declaration_made_conclusive: The law makes an executive declaration that the acquisition is for a public purpose conclusive evidence of that fact.

issues.definition: When a public-acquisition proceeding concerns a law that makes an executive declaration conclusive evidence of public purpose, the conclusive-declaration provision is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A law enacted shortly before the Constitution commenced is not exempt from the constitutional compensation requirement merely because it is an existing law; the specified presidential certification is required.
material_facts: The challenged State law was enacted within eighteen months before the Constitution commenced.
The law had not been submitted for, or received, presidential certification.
The State argued that the law was saved as an existing law even without certification.
issues.conclusion: The law was not saved from Article 31(2) by Article 31(5), because it had not received the certification required by Article 31(6).
issues.legal_principle: Articles 31(5) and 31(6), read together, save existing laws enacted more than eighteen months before the Constitution commenced under Article 31(5), while a State law enacted within that eighteen-month period must be submitted to the President and certified under Article 31(6) to receive the specified protection. Reading Article 31(5) to save an uncertified law from that period would make Article 31(6) redundant.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_law: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a State law.
predicates.enacted_shortly_before_constitution: The State law was enacted within the period shortly before the Constitution commenced to which the certification requirement applies.
predicates.not_presidentially_certified: The law was not submitted for and did not receive the required presidential certification.

issues.definition: A State law challenged constitutionally, enacted within the specified pre-commencement period and not presidentially certified, is not exempt from the compensation requirement.

issues.legal_issue: Legislative principles for determining compensation for acquired property must provide a just equivalent of what the owner has lost, and whether they do so is subject to judicial review.
material_facts: The law prescribed principles for determining compensation for acquired land.
The State argued that the legislature could determine what indemnity was proper without requiring equivalence in value.
The compensation provision limited the amount payable by reference to a valuation date unrelated to when the land might be acquired.
issues.conclusion: The legislature may choose principles for determining compensation, but those principles must secure a just equivalent of the property taken; whether they account for the property’s true value and exclude irrelevant matters is a justiciable issue.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), read with Entry 42 of List III of the Seventh Schedule, permits legislative discretion in prescribing principles and the manner of payment, but requires the amount determined to be compensation—a just equivalent of what the owner is deprived of. The adequacy of the principles is for the courts to decide. The Australian decisions, including Grace Brothers Pty. Ltd. v. The Commonwealth, were distinguished because they concerned different constitutional language and protections.

predicates.constitutional_property_acquisition_chal: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.compensation_principles_specified: The law specifies principles for determining the amount payable for the property acquired.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns an acquisition law that specifies compensation principles, the adequacy of those principles is subject to judicial review.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation ceiling based on a historical market value that may bear no relation to the value when property is acquired is arbitrary and does not satisfy the constitutional compensation requirement.
material_facts: The challenged law was permanent and allowed land to be acquired many years after its enactment.
It capped compensation at the land’s market value on a fixed historical date, regardless of the value when acquisition occurred.
The value of land could increase substantially between the historical date and acquisition.
issues.conclusion: The provision capping compensation at the historical market value was unconstitutional and void.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2) requires compensation to be a just equivalent of the property taken. Although an earlier valuation date may be permissible in circumstances such as a known acquisition scheme causing a sharp anticipatory rise in prices, fixing a ceiling at a date that may have no relation to value at acquisition is arbitrary and fails to meet that requirement. The principles must account for the property’s true value and are subject to judicial review.

predicates.constitutional_property_acquisition_chal: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a law authorizing compulsory acquisition of property.
predicates.permanent_acquisition_law: The law remains in force and permits acquisitions at times substantially later than its enactment.
predicates.compensation_ceiling_uses_historical_val: The law caps compensation by reference to a past valuation that may bear no relation to the property's value when it is acquired.

issues.definition: In a constitutional challenge to a permanent acquisition law, a ceiling based on a historical value unrelated to value at acquisition is invalid.
